question: How does the march return before it regains its full force?
intro: A clipped march frames a middle section of sustained melody and flowing broken chords. In the composer’s recording, follow the quiet rebuilding of the march before its full return — and its unexpectedly light exit.

sections.label: Alla marcia
sections.mNote: short chordal attacks and a recurring march rhythm

sections.label: Singing middle · un poco meno mosso
sections.mNote: sustained upper melody above flowing left-hand arpeggios

sections.label: Rebuilding the march · approximate
sections.mNote: march rhythm reappears quietly and gains momentum

sections.label: Tempo I · march restored
sections.mNote: original rhythm returns at fuller dynamic weight

sections.label: Coda · a light exit
sections.mNote: the march dwindles into an ascending broken chord

cues.title: The gaps belong to the rhythm
cues.text: “Alla marcia” means in the manner of a march. Listen to the spaces between the short chords: the recurring pattern depends on released notes and rests, not on an unbroken stream of sound.
cues.evidence: Gutheil’s first edition, printed pp. 20–21, shows staccato chords, rests and repeated rhythmic cells. The analysis detects active attacks from the opening, but does not identify articulation note by note.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The fifth was written first
cues.text: The G minor Prelude was written in 1901, before the other nine pieces of Op. 23. Rachmaninoff played it in Moscow in February 1903, alongside the first two preludes of the collection.
cues.evidence: Composition and premiere history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude_in_G_minor_(Rachmaninoff). IMSLP’s catalogue separately records the set’s 10 February 1903 Moscow premiere.

cues.title: From detached to connected
cues.text: The middle passage exchanges the march’s short chords for a sustained upper melody and continuous left-hand arpeggios. Follow the long line while the accompaniment moves through a much wider span of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Gutheil score p. 22 begins Un poco meno mosso with the sustained upper line and wide left-hand broken chords. The analysis gives a boundary at 1:02 and a level decrease through 1:10, supporting a broad contrast rather than an exact first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer at Victor
cues.text: Rachmaninoff signed his first Victor contract in April 1920, after recording for Edison in 1919. This Prelude followed in May, near the beginning of the Victor association that continued for the rest of his life.
cues.evidence: RCA Complete Recordings booklet, “The Recordings”, dates the Victor contract to 21 April 1920 and describes the previous Edison sessions. DAHR dates matrix C-23984 take 4 to 17 May 1920.

cues.title: A rhythm before its full return
cues.text: Near the end of the middle passage, listen for the clipped march pattern beginning to replace the flowing accompaniment. The score rebuilds it quietly before restoring the original tempo and fuller chords.
cues.evidence: Gutheil score p. 23 moves from diminuendo and ritardando into a ppp march fragment marked poco a poco accelerando e cresc. al Tempo I. Analysis boundaries at 2:04 and 2:20 surround the quiet window at 2:10; alignment is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognise the march by its shape
cues.text: When the march has regained its weight, compare its recurring short-note pattern with the opening. The return is more than a louder passage: the same rhythmic profile restores a familiar way of organising the phrases.
cues.evidence: Gutheil score p. 24 marks Tempo I over the recovered march material. The analysis has a boundary at 2:26 and a sustained level increase from −17 dB at 2:25 to about −9 dB by 2:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An approved fourth take
cues.text: Victor’s register lists four takes of this Prelude across three May 1920 sessions. The released performance was take four, issued as Victor 74628, a twelve-inch record; the earlier attempts were not all made on the same day.
cues.evidence: DAHR lists takes 1–2 on 3 May, take 3 on 4 May and master take 4 on 17 May, with the Victor issue: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/700009183. The RCA booklet identifies the reissued take as C-23984-4.

cues.title: A march that does not stamp shut
cues.text: The ending reduces the march to lighter fragments, then a quick rising broken chord and a short final note. Follow the thinning attacks: Rachmaninoff closes by taking weight away, not by adding one last heavy chord.
cues.evidence: Gutheil score p. 25 ends with diminuendo, pp leggiero and a rising arpeggio into a short high G. The analysis marks a boundary at 3:20 and a rapid decay after 3:25; it does not fix the last note within two seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clipped chords yield to a continuous line
transitions.how: The opening march descends and diminishes until its clipped gestures have lost their earlier weight. Un poco meno mosso then changes the texture: a connected upper melody rides above broad left-hand arpeggios. The harmony is now spread through each beat rather than struck in short blocks. The contrast depends on articulation, spacing and continuity as much as on the quieter dynamic.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition pp. 21–22 supplies the diminuendo and Un poco meno mosso: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c9/IMSLP105592-PMLP02017-Rachmaninov_-_23_-_10_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf. The 1:02 boundary and subsequent level reduction support the estimated join.

transitions.title: The march returns almost under its breath
transitions.how: The singing passage slows and diminishes; its running accompaniment contracts into a closing figure. A fragment of the march then enters ppp. Rachmaninoff writes a gradual acceleration and crescendo towards Tempo I, so the rhythm can be recognised before the opening’s speed and weight have returned. Chromatically shifting chords make this a passage of preparation, not yet the stable restatement.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 23 shows dim. e rit., the ppp march figure and poco a poco accelerando e cresc. al Tempo I. The 2:04 boundary and low level at 2:10 locate this transitional region approximately.

transitions.title: The prepared rhythm regains its weight
transitions.how: The same short-note figure continues through the acceleration rather than stopping for a fresh start. At Tempo I the original march material is restored with a forte marking and a further crescendo. What was tentative in the link becomes a full statement: continuity of rhythm connects the sections while the growing dynamic distinguishes preparation from arrival.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 23–24 joins the acceleration directly to Tempo I and forte. The 2:26 boundary and level rise across 2:25–2:35 support this approximate restoration point.

transitions.title: The march dissolves into a rising figure
transitions.how: The march fragments descend and lose volume. Rachmaninoff then removes most of the chordal weight: pp leggiero introduces a short broken-chord sweep across the registers, ending on a detached high G. The closing gesture retains motion but not the march’s mass, so the tonic arrives without a final fortissimo block.
transitions.evidence: The last three systems of score p. 25 supply diminuendo, pp leggiero and the rising figure. The analysis boundary at 3:20, level drop after 3:15 and near-silence after 3:30 place the close broadly.

The exact first-publication day remains unknown. composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky
Mamontov’s Moscow Private Russian Opera, 1897–98 · Bolshoi Theatre, 1904–06
Ivanovka near Tambov · Dresden · New York · Villa Senar, Lake Lucerne · Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
